introHtml: Definitions for the scientific, legal, and engineering terms used throughout the stories about Lake Conestee and its dam.

entries.definitionHtml: Bottomland hardwood forests are river swamps. They are found along rivers and streams in the southeastern and south-central United States, generally in broad floodplains. These ecosystems are commonly found wherever streams or rivers at least occasionally cause flooding beyond their channel confines (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: Establishes the basic structure for regulating discharges of pollutants into the waters of the United States and regulating quality standards for surface waters. The basis of the CWA was enacted in 1948 and was called the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, but the Act was significantly reorganized and expanded in 1972. "Clean Water Act" became the Act's common name with amendments in 1972 (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: Concentrations of a contaminant in soil, sediment, or water that are used as an early check for possible harm to plants and animals. Measured levels at a site are compared to these values. A contaminant that exceeds its value is flagged for closer study; it is not automatically considered harmful. Screening values are a first step, not cleanup levels (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: A broad group of more than 30 elements that can harm people and other living things, some at very low concentrations. They occur naturally in many geologic settings and are also released by industry, including textile manufacturing, electroplating, metal finishing, and the burning of coal and other fuels. Some, such as zinc, copper, and chromium, are needed by humans and other organisms in tiny amounts but are harmful at higher levels. Others, including lead, cadmium, arsenic, and mercury, serve no beneficial role in the body, can build up over time, and can cause organ damage, immune effects, and cancer (EPA). Heavy metals cling to sediment particles and tend to stay bound to riverbed sediments indefinitely, as long as the sediment is left undisturbed.

Exceeding a screening value is a signal to look closer; these values are not cleanup standards (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: A hard surface area that either prevents or retards the entry of water into the soil mantle or causes water to run off the surface in greater quantities or at an increased rate of flow. Common impervious surfaces include rooftops, walkways, patios, driveways, parking lots, storage areas, concrete or asphalt paving, and compacted gravel roads (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: A type of sluice gate or flow control device typically installed in open channels or pipelines to regulate the flow of water or other fluids. It can be raised, lowered, or sealed off completely to control, direct, or stop the movement of water (Enke Group).

entries.definitionHtml: Commonly known as ‘forever chemicals,’ this group of more than 10,000 man-made compounds has been manufactured since the 1940s and is now found throughout the environment and in living things, including people. PFAS are used in non-stick cookware, waterproof and fire-resistant clothing, stain-resistant carpets, food packaging, and firefighting foam. They are extremely persistent and accumulate in blood, tissues, soil, sediment, water, and wildlife. They are associated with reproductive and developmental effects, cancer risk, weakened immune systems, and metabolic disruption (EPA). In 2024, EPA listed two of the most common, PFOS and PFOA, as hazardous substances, and drinking water limits for them are now as low as 4 ng/L (parts per trillion).

entries.definitionHtml: A porous surface area that allows rainwater to soak naturally into the ground, reducing stormwater runoff and filtering out pollutants. Common pervious surfaces include grassy areas, gardens, permeable pavers, unpaved walkways, and mulch.

entries.definitionHtml: Chemical or biological substances used to kill or control pests such as weeds, insects, rodents, and fungi. Many also affect organisms they weren't meant to target, and they and their breakdown products can build up in soils, sediments, and living things. Many pesticides are persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic, concentrating as they move up the food chain, and some are harmful at extremely low concentrations. Several, such as DDT and other organochlorines, are now banned. Effects on people vary by pesticide but include poisoning, nervous system and cognitive effects, reproductive harm, birth defects, endocrine disruption, and cancer (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: Chlorinated chemicals used from the 1930s in electrical transformers and capacitors because they insulate well, and also in textile processing, flame retardants, plastics, adhesives, paints, caulking, and hydraulic systems. US production was halted in the late 1970s, but PCBs resist breakdown and persist for decades, mostly bound up in sediments and soils. They are persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic, and are linked to reproductive, developmental, neurological, and immune effects, endocrine disruption, and cancer in people and animals (EPA).

entries.definitionHtml: A group of hundreds of carbon-based chemicals, 16 of which are designated priority pollutants because of their toxicity, persistence, and widespread presence. They come mainly from burning coal, petroleum, and other fuels, and are found in coal tar, coal gas, coal ash, creosote, road and roofing tar, asphalt, and petroleum products. Effects depend on the type, but PAHs can harm the skin, body fluids, and immune system, and several are known carcinogens (CDC). They bind tightly to soil and sediment particles, where they can persist for decades.

entries.definitionHtml: When water slows down, such as when it flows from a creek into a lake, suspended sediment can drop out of suspension and settle on the lake bed. This is known as sedimentation, and when sedimentation rates are high and the sediment collects in a lake bed, this can lead to lake infilling, where the volume of the lake shrinks as it is filled with sediment (USGS).
